text: Lesson 26 covered anticipating the hard questions. This lesson is about what you actually say once one of those questions lands squarely on a tradeoff you chose on purpose, for a stated reason -- not something the team simply overlooked.

Consider two sentences describing the same technical fact: no failover for a given service. 'We didn't think about failover for that service' is a gap. 'We chose not to build failover, because the service is non-critical and the engineering cost didn't justify it' is a decision. A review board can't tell those apart from the architecture diagram alone -- the only thing that distinguishes a gap from a deliberate tradeoff is what you say when it's questioned, which is exactly why writing the reasoning into the ADR at decision time matters: you're reading a defense back, not inventing one under pressure.

A three-part pattern makes that defense concrete. First, restate the actual constraint that drove the decision -- a launch date, a budget, a data volume that didn't justify the overhead -- before defending the choice itself. Second, name the alternative you didn't take and its specific cost in real numbers: the percentage cost increase, the weeks of engineering time, measured against the availability target your chosen design already meets. Third, invite the counter-proposal -- tell the board that if the requirements have genuinely changed, you want to hear what changed, which puts the burden on them to name something concrete rather than asking you to re-justify a sound call against vague discomfort.

Three habits reliably make a sound tradeoff look weak in the room: getting defensive, which invites the board to dig in even when the decision was reasonable; relitigating every option from scratch instead of stating the one reason that actually mattered; and conceding to 'reconsider' just to end the discomfort of being questioned, which trains the room to treat every future tradeoff you present as negotiable.

Defending a tradeoff well doesn't mean never changing your mind -- it means only changing it in response to something that actually changed, not in response to the discomfort of being asked. Next lesson picks up from there: what a review board's feedback actually looks like once the meeting ends, and how to revise a design around it without losing the original intent you walked in with.
